newsitem.title: GERMANY: German leader says Russian Jewish emigration slows.
newsitem.headline: German leader says Russian Jewish emigration slows.

text.p: The leader of Germany's Jewish community was quoted on Monday as saying that a recent surge of Jewish immigrants to Germany from Russia had slowed with greater political stability there, but numbers from Ukraine had risen.

Ignatz Bubis, chairman of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, told the magazine Main City that overall the number of Jewish immigrants from the former Soviet Union to Germany had slowed this year compared to previous years.
Over the past six years, the magazine said Germany's Jewish population had grown by one-third to about 50,000, mostly through immigration from the former Soviet Union.

"The number of immigrants is decreasing and this is mostly due to the fact that the political situation in Russia has stabilised somewhat," Bubis, 69, told the magazine which is published by the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.

"But in the Ukraine there is more political instability and we have seen slightly more people coming from there. As political conditions improve, the flow of immigrants will also decrease," he told the English-language magazine.

Bubis, who was born in Poland and came to Germany after World War Two with hopes of emigrating to Israel or the United States, said the number of Jewish emigrants from the former Soviet Union who were seeking to go to the United States or Israel was also slowing.
He said Israeli officials were upset with the efforts of Jews in Germany to attract more immigrants.

"The Israelis are actually angry at us, saying that we are drawing people away from Israel. That is simply not true. A better question is why do they come to Germany of all places and not America or Israel," Bubis said.

Bubis said Jews seeking to live in Germany probably had a cultural affinity with the country. But he noted that eight times as many Jewish immigrants go to the U.S. than to Germany and 15 times as many go to Israel.
Jews seeking to immigrate emigrate to Germany must show that they have suffered religious persecution.
Bubis said authorities were cracking down on people falsifying documents to claim they were of Jewish heritage in order to leave the former Soviet Union.
"There have certainly been many attempts and some have been successful," he said, noting the problem had also affected Israel. "Individual cases and their paperwork are being more closely checked."
Asked if many Jews would find it inconceivable to live in Germany because of past anti-Semitism, Bubis said that for Jews to hate Germans would be against Jewish tradition.
"And to simply hate someone because they are German would mean that I would be just like the Nazis," Bubis said.
